prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It will be a while before recollections in tranquility set in, as time in its adversary mode of darker days ticks on transfixing you in newsprint. It will be a while before those sudden winds descend upon the Po. A while before the laughter echoes in the dark; before the sounds of seagulls and accordions, harmonicas mix in those parting shots of long-forgotten flicks with names like La notte brava, I Pugni in tasca, L’oro di Napoli. Your show-offy had intelligence; not the “unconscious” your friend Calvino claims you lacked. Ha-ha. It will be a while before the tranquility comes round again. A while before you’re able to get up and move about; stare out from your Swallow’s Nest on those dappled waters of Salerno’s Gulf, almost fable-like. “Didn’t it go by awfully fast?” your buddy Howard once sweetly asked. It will be a while and sometimes more and not your last.

outputs.L1:
It will be some time before recollections in tranquility take hold, as time, in its adversarial guise of darker days, ticks on, transfixing you in newsprint. It will be some time before those sudden winds descend upon the Po; some time before laughter echoes in the dark; before the cries of seagulls mingle with accordions and harmonicas in those parting shots of long-forgotten films bearing names like *La notte brava*, *I Pugni in tasca*, and *L’oro di Napoli*. Your show-offiness had intelligence—not the “unconscious” your friend Calvino claimed you lacked. Ha-ha.

It will be some time before tranquility returns. Some time before you are able to rise and move about; to gaze out from your Swallow’s Nest upon the dappled waters of the Gulf of Salerno, almost fable-like. “Didn’t it go by awfully fast?” your buddy Howard once asked, sweetly. It will be some time—and sometimes longer—and not your last.
outputs.L2:
Peaceful remembrance will not arrive for some time; meanwhile, time, turned hostile in these dark days, keeps moving, holding you fixed inside the printed news. It will be some time before abrupt gusts sweep down over the Po. Some time before laughter rings out in the darkness; before cries of gulls, accordions, and harmonicas blend with the farewell images of half-remembered old films bearing titles such as *La notte brava*, *I Pugni in tasca*, and *L’oro di Napoli*. Your flamboyance had intellect behind it—not the “unconscious” that your friend Calvino said you did not possess. Ha-ha.

Serenity will take time to return. It will be a while before you can rise and walk around again; before you can look out from your Swallow’s Nest at the speckled waters of the Gulf of Salerno, nearly like something from a fable. “Didn’t it all pass terribly quickly?” your friend Howard once asked with tenderness. It will take time—sometimes even longer—and it will not be the final time.

The speaker suggests that the return of peaceful reflection will not be immediate. In the present moment, the days feel darker and more difficult, marked by heaviness, uncertainty, or fatigue. Calm thought, the kind that allows one to look at life with distance and clarity, seems temporarily out of reach. Yet the speaker does not present this as a permanent loss. Rather, peace is imagined as something that may slowly come back with time, after the harshness of the present has passed.

Throughout the passage, memory plays a central role. The speaker recalls places, sounds, films, and companions as fragments of a vivid cultural past. These memories do not appear in a fixed or orderly sequence; instead, they linger like flashes of experience: a city, a voice, a melody, a cinema, a shared conversation. Together, they evoke a rich world of artistic and intellectual life. The past is not simply remembered as a set of events, but as an atmosphere made up of friendships, images, ideas, and sensations that continue to resonate.

The text also reflects on intelligence and friendship, especially through the speaker’s playful disagreement with Calvino’s judgment. This disagreement does not seem hostile; it is affectionate and lively, the kind of debate that can exist between people who respect one another. By questioning or gently opposing Calvino’s view, the speaker reveals an intellectual independence, but also a sense of intimacy with the cultural circle being remembered. Thought, in this passage, is not abstract or isolated. It is connected to friendship, conversation, wit, and the pleasure of differing opinions.

At the same time, the speaker imagines a future in which the ability to move freely, observe the world, and recover tranquility will return. There is a quiet hope in this vision. To move again is not merely a physical act; it also suggests reentering life, becoming attentive once more to surroundings, details, landscapes, and people. Observation becomes a path back to calm. The speaker seems to believe that, eventually, the mind will regain its openness and the world will again become something to contemplate rather than simply endure.

Overall, the passage conveys a bittersweet awareness of time’s speed. Life and experience appear to have passed quickly, leaving behind brilliant but incomplete traces. There is melancholy in this recognition, because so much has already gone by and can only be recovered through memory. Yet the tone is not entirely despairing. The speaker understands that life is not finished, that perception, movement, thought, and friendship may still continue in some form. The result is a delicate mixture of sadness and hope: an acknowledgment of loss, but also a belief that there remains something more to see, to feel, and to understand.
outputs.L4:
You will not be calm at once. That is the first thing you must understand. After the dark times, after the rooms where no one spoke plainly, after the long corridors of grief and the nights in which even sleep seemed to remember too much, calm will not arrive like a door flung open. It will come late, if it comes at all. It will come in fragments: in the pale wash of morning on a wall, in the sound of a cup placed carefully on a table, in the sudden scent of rain rising from stone.

You will think, perhaps, that you have forgotten how to live. You will think that the self you once carried so easily has been misplaced somewhere—on a road, in a station, beside a sea you crossed too quickly. But memory is patient. It waits beneath the visible world. It waits in the dust of old streets, in the afternoon light falling across shutters, in the face of a friend you have not seen for years and yet recognize immediately. It waits in black-and-white images from Italian films: a woman turning her head in a piazza, a man walking away down a sunlit road, the silence after music, the tremor before departure. You will remember these things not because they are yours exactly, but because they have become part of the way you understand loss.

And you will return, in thought if not in body, to those landscapes that seem to have been made for recollection: hills silvered with olive trees, villages clinging to stone, the sea spreading out beyond a terrace like a promise no one can keep. You will see cypresses, dry grass, laundry moving in a warm wind. You will hear a motorbike passing far below. You will remember youth, or what you called youth at the time, though it was already full of farewells. You will remember wanting to become an artist, or at least wanting to live as though art could save something from disappearance. Perhaps it did. Perhaps it still does.

You will say to yourself: later. Later I will understand. Later I will forgive. Later the noise will settle. And later will become its own country, one you approach slowly, carrying what remains. The mind does not heal in a straight line. It circles. It repeats. It returns to the same image until the image softens. It speaks again and again the names of the dead, the absent, the distant, not to summon them back, but to keep them from vanishing completely.

Life, meanwhile, will continue at its terrible speed. Years will pass with the quickness of a cut in a film. One moment you are young and standing in the heat outside a cinema; the next you are older, looking at photographs, astonished by the faces of those who once seemed permanent. Friends will scatter, return, disappear, write, fall silent, reappear with changed voices. Some will remain faithful in ways you did not expect. Some will become part of the landscape of your life, like a bridge, a church bell, a road leading down to water.

And because everything passes so quickly, what endures will seem almost unbearable in its tenderness: friendship, art, a remembered street, the particular blue of evening over a familiar town. You will understand that places keep faith with us differently than people do. They do not console, exactly, but they remain available to memory. A square, a hill, a coastline, a room with a window open to the heat—these become witnesses. They hold the versions of ourselves we can no longer be.

So calm will come, but slowly. Peace will return not as triumph, not as forgetting, but as a quieter form of attention. You will sit somewhere in the late light and feel, for a moment, that the world has not been restored, but it has become bearable. You will think of the films, the friends, the landscapes, the griefs that shaped you. You will feel how much has gone, and how much, strangely, remains. And in that fragile pause, before the next wave of memory, you will almost be calm.

A Napoli, città di contrasti e passione, ogni strada racconta una storia fatta di voci, colori e gesti intensi. Tra i vicoli stretti e il profumo del mare, anche una parola dura come **pugni** può trasformarsi in simbolo di forza, resistenza e voglia di rialzarsi.

I pugni non sono solo segno di scontro: possono rappresentare la determinazione di chi lotta per i propri sogni, di chi affronta le difficoltà quotidiane senza perdere il sorriso. A **Napoli**, questa energia si sente ovunque: nei mercati affollati, nei quartieri popolari, nelle piazze dove la vita scorre veloce e autentica.

“**Your**” diventa allora un invito personale: la tua storia, la tua forza, il tuo modo di vivere Napoli. Perché ogni persona porta con sé una battaglia, un ricordo, una speranza. E in una città così viva, anche i pugni chiusi possono aprirsi, diventando mani pronte a costruire, abbracciare e ricominciare.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, poetic prose paragraph in the style of a late-modernist elegy, addressing an aging Italian filmmaker and weaving in references to Calvino, Howard, Salerno, the Po, and old Italian films.
counterfactuals.output: Maestro, as the light thins over your hands and the reels grow brittle in their tin reliquaries, you sit among the ghosts of old Italian films like a custodian of weather: Calvino’s invisible cities rising and dissolving behind your eyelids, Howard’s remembered voice crossing the Atlantic in a grain of static, Salerno shining with its harbor of salt and departures, and the Po moving northward through fog as if dragging all of childhood behind it. Once you taught faces to endure the camera’s mercy—the widow at the shutter, the boy with dust on his shoes, the priest, the thief, the woman laughing before history entered the room—and now the images return not as triumphs but as small, wounded birds, beating against the dark auditorium of the blood. O aging maker of rain-streaked piazzas and noon bells, of kisses held too long beneath Fascist walls, of bicycles, breadlines, saints, actresses, and soldiers vanishing into silver nitrate, you have outlived the beautiful lie of continuity: the cut has become the law, the splice the only prayer. Yet still, in the last projection, when the screen trembles and the lamp coughs gold, Italy gathers again—river, city, mother, cinema—while you, half shadow, half witness, lean toward the flicker as though toward a final shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical second-person meditation on memory, illness, and cinema, with the repeated phrase “It will be a while,” including allusions to La notte brava, I Pugni in tasca, and L’oro di Napoli.
counterfactuals.output:
You wake with the room already remembering you.

The glass of water beside the bed has gathered a little dust, a little moonlight, a little proof that the night went on without asking your permission. Your body is slow to return from wherever illness sends it: that dim republic of fever, corridors, murmured instructions, the white grammar of sheets. You lie still and listen to the pipes, the traffic, a bird rehearsing one note until it becomes almost human.

It will be a while, you tell yourself.

A while before the body becomes ordinary again. Before the stairs stop being mountains. Before a spoon, lifted to the mouth, is only a spoon and not an expedition. Before memory ceases to arrive in fragments, like a damaged reel: a streetlamp, a hand on your shoulder, the bad coffee of a station bar, the face of someone you loved half-turned toward a window.

Cinema taught you this kind of haunting. Not the grand declaration, not the music swelling like a tide, but the afterimage: boys moving through the Roman night in *La notte brava*, reckless and already lost, their laughter thin as cigarette smoke; the clenched rooms and inward violence of *I Pugni in tasca*, where the family house feels less like shelter than a skull; the Naples of *L’oro di Napoli*, glittering and hungry, comic and wounded, as if poverty itself had learned to sing through its teeth.

You remember them not as plots but as temperatures.

A hot street.
A shuttered room.
A card table.
A balcony.
A face eating in silence.
A face about to betray itself.

It will be a while.

You have begun to understand that memory is not an archive but an illness with good days and bad days. Some mornings it lets you rise, wash, dress, and pass for someone intact. Other mornings it lays a cool hand on your chest and says: no, today we return. Today you will stand again in the kitchen where the telephone rang. Today you will smell disinfectant under the sweetness of oranges. Today the dead will be practical and close, asking where you put the keys.

And you, obedient projectionist, thread the film.

There you are as a child, not yet aware of the body as a future betrayal. There you are in the dark of a theater, your face lit by other people’s sorrow. There you are outside afterward, stunned by ordinary weather. The world, having ended beautifully for ninety minutes, resumes its errands. Buses gasp at the curb. Lovers quarrel under posters. Someone sweeps popcorn into a pan with the melancholy of a priest.

You walk home carrying borrowed destinies.

It will be a while, you say again, and the phrase becomes less a warning than a lullaby.

Illness has slowed the film. It has made you notice the splice, the grain, the trembling edge of every frame. You see how the living move through scenes they cannot interpret until years later, if ever. You see how suffering sometimes enters like a minor character and then refuses to leave. You see how comedy and grief share the same doorway, as in Naples, where a joke may hide a wound and a wound may wear a gold ring.

You have been angry at your body for becoming visible. For insisting on its weight, its fluids, its negotiations. You preferred it when it was merely the instrument of your longing, the vehicle of your errands, the faithful animal carrying you from one desire to the next. Now it is the landscape itself: uncertain, weathered, full of closed roads.

Be patient, the old films whisper, though they were never patient themselves. They rushed toward ruin, toward dawn, toward the slap, the kiss, the inheritance, the sea. Their faces are young forever and still they suffer. Their nights never end and still morning waits just beyond the cut.

It will be a while.

So you practice the small ceremonials of return. You open the curtains. You let the room enter you. You swallow the medicine with water that tastes faintly of metal and sleep. You sit in the chair by the window and watch the street compose itself: a woman with bread, a child dragging a red bag, a dog pausing with philosophical seriousness at the curb.

Nothing happens, and because nothing happens, you are grateful.

Memory comes, but softer now. It sits beside you rather than on your chest. It does not ask to be believed completely. It shows you a scene and lets the edges blur. Perhaps you were happy there. Perhaps you only remember the light. Perhaps the light has done the work of mercy, gilding what could not be saved.

The cinema inside you flickers.

You are the city after midnight.
You are the fist in the pocket.
You are the gold that is not gold, the hunger dressed as luck.
You are the audience and the screen, the wound and the radiance passing over it.

It will be a while.

But the reel has not run out.  
The lamp is still burning.  
Somewhere, behind your eyes, the next frame waits.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short experimental prose piece that sounds like an art-film obituary: nostalgic, fragmented, intellectual, and full of Italian coastal imagery, literary references, and melancholy humor.
counterfactuals.output:
He died, as he had lived, slightly out of focus.

The Ligurian sea kept arriving in small revisions, blue, then green, then the color of a bruise remembered by Proust. On the quay, widows in black sunglasses shelled prawns with the severity of minor philosophers. Someone said his last words were “more lemon,” but this may have been apocryphal, or merely lunch.

He had loved ruins: Roman baths, failed marriages, the footnotes of German editions. In youth he wore linen and quoted Leopardi to women who preferred scooters. Later, in Naples, he developed a theory that all history was just laundry strung between balconies—white shirts, red underthings, the exhausted flags of private republics.

At the funeral, the priest mispronounced his name. A gull laughed, or committed an act of criticism. The coffin gleamed like a badly restored baroque cabinet. We followed it uphill past caper bushes, chipped Madonnas, boys kicking a ball against eternity.

He once claimed the Adriatic was more intelligent than the Tyrrhenian, “but less sensual.” This was after three grappas and before the argument about Dante’s exile, Fellini’s fog, and whether anchovies possess a tragic consciousness. He forgave everyone eventually, except Visconti for being right too often.

Now the house is shuttered. The lemons drop of their own accord. His books smell of salt, mildew, and marginal objections. In one volume of Calvino, a pressed bougainvillea has become a small purple ghost.

We remember him walking away from us down the beach at dusk, trousers rolled, shoes in hand, as if testing the temperature of oblivion.

It was cold, he reported.

But beautifully lit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a paragraph imitating John Ashbery’s associative, elegiac style, about someone waiting for tranquility and recollection to return after dark days, with mentions of Calvino and classic Italian movies.
counterfactuals.output: After the dark days had folded themselves like damp newspapers under the door, he waited for tranquility and recollection to come back—not together, perhaps, but in that slightly embarrassed procession by which lost things re-enter a room. Calvino was on the table, all invisible staircases and cities remembering him better than he remembered himself, while on the television the old Italian movies drifted past in silver weather: a bicycle, a fountain, a woman turning away as if history had called her by the wrong name. He thought peace might arrive as a small provincial train, late but forgiven, carrying faces from afternoons he had mislaid; or else as the pause after music in a courtyard no one owned. Meanwhile the shadows kept rearranging the furniture, kindly now, almost ceremonially, and he sat among them, practicing the difficult art of being ready for what had once been simple.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal reflective monologue addressed to a bedridden artist, mixing memories of newsprint, seagulls, accordions, the Gulf of Salerno, and a friend named Howard asking, “Didn’t it go by awfully fast?”
counterfactuals.output:
You lie there like a canvas that has refused the wall, old friend—stretched, pale, luminous in the dim room, while the afternoon folds itself around your bed with the patience of a nurse and the cruelty of a critic. Your hands, those restless birds, are still now on the sheet. But I know what they remember. Charcoal. Turpentine. The small violence of a line becoming a face. The way blue, properly wounded, can become evening.

Do you remember the newsprint?

Not the news itself—no one remembers that, not truly. Wars flattened into columns, ministers smiling through halftone fog, disasters already yellowing before the ink dried. I mean the paper: the gray softness of it, the smell of rain and coal dust, the way it blackened our thumbs as if it were taking our fingerprints for some future trial. You used to spread old newspapers across the studio floor before painting, and by morning the headlines had absorbed drips of cadmium red and ochre, so that history appeared to be bleeding beautifully and by accident.

Once, a photograph of a drowned city lay under your easel. By noon, you had spilled white paint across it, and it looked like seagulls had descended in a frenzy.

Ah, the seagulls.

They are outside your window now, though we are nowhere near the sea. Don’t argue; illness loosens geography. They come dragging the Gulf of Salerno behind them like a torn silk curtain. I can hear them screaming over the tiled roofs, flashing like scraps of bone against that enormous southern light. We were there, weren’t we? Or perhaps we only invented it from postcards and hunger. The Gulf curved below us, blue as a saint’s robe, and the boats moved so slowly they seemed to be thinking. Lemons burned in the trees. Somewhere an old man played an accordion badly, which is to say honestly, and the whole coast breathed in and out like a sleeping animal.

You said then that the sea was impossible to paint because it had no face.

I said that was why it was always posing.

The accordion kept wheezing from the café, a little lung full of sorrow and red wine. It played as if memory itself had buttons: press here for childhood, here for betrayal, here for the mother standing in a doorway, here for the first rented room with a mattress, a skylight, and a certainty that genius would arrive before winter. The music walked crookedly through the square, climbed the steps, entered our glasses, and by evening even the shadows were swaying.

You laughed. I can still see it. Your head thrown back, your eyes wet from the sun, your shirt stained with anchovy oil and ultramarine. You were young enough then to believe exhaustion was proof of seriousness. We all were. We mistook hunger for discipline, confusion for depth, love for rescue. We thought art would save us from time, when in fact it merely taught us how to watch time sharpen its knives.

And Howard—do you remember Howard? Of course you do. Howard with his soft hat and his catastrophic shoes, always arriving late but with the expression of a man who had discovered the secret staircase behind reality. He bought three newspapers every morning and read none of them completely. He said the unfinished stories kept him hopeful. He had a laugh like a chair breaking in another room.

Years later, when his beard had gone white at the edges and his hands trembled slightly around his coffee cup, he leaned toward me and asked, “Didn’t it go by awfully fast?”

As if life were a train we had expected to board properly but instead had only glimpsed from the platform—windows lit, faces passing, someone in the dining car lifting a glass. Didn’t it go by awfully fast? The question has never stopped moving through me. It circles like a gull over refuse and revelation. It opens every door and finds the same room behind it.

I want to tell you no. I want to tell you it was long—magnificently, mercilessly long. Long as the drying of oil paint. Long as a fever night. Long as waiting for a letter from someone too proud to write. But Howard was right. The years collapsed like wet newsprint. Whole decades folded under the arm and carried off. Exhibitions, arguments, marriages, winters, the dead—compressed into a bundle tied with string, tossed at dawn onto the steps of some stranger’s house.

And now here you are, bedridden artist, monarch of pillows, exiled from your studio yet surrounded by invisible work. Do not think the paintings have stopped. They are continuing without you in the corners. The ceiling is preparing a retrospective. The cracks in the plaster have become rivers, roads, veins. Your blanket is a mountain range under snow. The water glass on the table contains the Gulf of Salerno in miniature, and if you look carefully, you will see a boat no larger than a fingernail crossing toward evening.

The accordion begins again.

It is under the bed. No, it is inside your chest. No, it is the bed itself breathing in pleats and sighs, squeezing out one tune after another from the old repertoire: the smell of newsprint, the cry of seagulls, Howard’s question, the Gulf shining below us like a promise no one knew how to keep.

Listen. The room is not a room anymore. It is a harbor. Your bed is a white boat. The sheet is a sail. The newspapers rise from the floor and flap into wings, each headline transformed into a bird, each obituary into a cloud. They circle above you, not accusing, not forgiving, only making that wild salt sound that means land is near or land is gone.

And you, who spent your life trying to catch the visible before it vanished, must know this now: nothing vanishes cleanly. Everything leaves a stain. Ink on thumb. Light on water. Music in the ribs. A friend’s voice in the corridor of the mind, asking his terrible, tender question.

Didn’t it go by awfully fast?

Yes, Howard. Yes. But not so fast that we failed to see it glitter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
